arXiv:2607.14087v2 [math.PR] 20 Jul 2026

Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture

Abhijeet Mulgund ††thanks: This work was supported by NSF under awards 2240532 and 2217023. Affiliation: University of Illinois Chicago Email: mulgund2@uic.edu
Abstract

We prove a stochastic comparison for Gaussian maxima. Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix satisfying R−𝟏𝟏𝖳/m⪰0R-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}/m\succeq 0, let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R), and let Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} be independent standard Gaussian random variables. Then

max1≤i≤mXi≤stmax1≤i≤mZi,\max_{1\leq i\leq m}X_{i}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}Z_{i},

or equivalently, ℙ{Xi≤c for every i}≥Φ(c)m\mathbb{P}\{X_{i}\leq c\text{ for every }i\}\geq\Phi(c)^{m} for every c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. This comparison resolves the Weak Simplex Conjecture: among d+1d+1 equiprobable equal-energy signals in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} transmitted over an additive white Gaussian noise channel, the regular simplex maximizes the probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding at every signal-to-noise ratio. It also proves the mean-width inequality asserted by the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture. In the deterministic no-feedback AWGN model with equiprobable messages, an unrestricted number of channel uses, and a maximal per-codeword total-energy constraint, it gives the exact optimal finite-energy performance. The proof combines a Gaussian product inequality for log-concave functions with an adaptive tilting argument that makes the inequality applicable to the one-sided threshold events defining the maximum. A lean formalization of this argument is available at https://github.com/abhmul/weak-simplex-conjecture-lean.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 60E15; Secondary 52A40, 94A24, 94B70.

Keywords. Gaussian maxima, stochastic domination, Gaussian inequalities, Weak Simplex Conjecture, simplex mean width, AWGN codes.

1 Introduction

1.1 Main theorem and consequences

The Weak Simplex Conjecture traces back to an observation of Shannon reported by Rice in 1950 [31]; the name was later coined by Massey in 1988 [20]. It asks how to place m=d+1m=d+1 equiprobable signals of equal energy in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} when the channel adds isotropic Gaussian noise and the receiver uses maximum-likelihood decoding. The conjecture asserts that a regular simplex is optimal at every signal-to-noise ratio. If the unit signal vectors are x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} and G=(⟨xi,xj⟩)i,jG=(\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle)_{i,j} is their Gram matrix, then the average probability of correct decoding satisfies

Pc​(x1,…,xm,λ)=e−λ2/2m​𝔼​exp⁡{λ​max1≤i≤m​ξi},ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G).P_{\mathrm{c}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m};\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\xi_{i}\right\},\qquad\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G). (1)

Thus the coding problem is an extremal problem for the moment-generating function (MGF) of a Gaussian maximum.

Our main theorem is a distributional comparison obtained after adding the same independent Gaussian random variable to all coordinates and rescaling. Let J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}. If RR is a correlation matrix satisfying

R−1m​J⪰0,R-\frac{1}{m}J\succeq 0, (2)

then, for X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R) and independent standard Gaussian random variables Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m},

ℙ{maxiXi≤c}≥Φ(c)m=ℙ{maxiZi≤c}(c∈ℝ).\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{i}X_{i}\leq c\right\}\geq\Phi(c)^{m}=\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{i}Z_{i}\leq c\right\}\qquad(c\in\mathbb{R}). (3)

Equivalently, maxi⁡Xi\max_{i}X_{i} is first-order stochastically dominated by the independent maximum. The event on the left is the equal-threshold lower orthant (−∞,c]m(-\infty,c]^{m}; no comparison for arbitrary threshold vectors is claimed.

The semidefinite condition in (2) is exactly the condition produced by the coding problem. For every correlation matrix GG, define

R=m−1m​G+1m​J.R=\frac{m-1}{m}G+\frac{1}{m}J. (4)

Then R−J/m⪰0R-J/m\succeq 0, and the regular-simplex covariance mm−1​(I−J/m)\frac{m}{m-1}(I-J/m) is mapped to ImI_{m}. Moreover, if μ>0\mu>0 and λ=(m−1)/m​μ\lambda=\sqrt{(m-1)/m}\,\mu, then

e−μ2/2𝔼eμ​maxi​Xi=e−λ2/2𝔼eλ​maxi​ξi.e^{-\mu^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\max_{i}X_{i}}=e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}. (5)

Consequently, (3) gives the MGF comparison required by (1). It resolves the Weak Simplex Conjecture, implies the expected-maximum inequality and hence the mean-width inequality asserted by the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture, and yields an exact finite-energy AWGN formula when no restriction is imposed on the number of channel uses.

To the best of our knowledge, the present paper gives the first complete proof of the Weak Simplex Conjecture in all dimensions and at every signal-to-noise ratio. The same argument proves the optimal-value inequality in the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture; it does not determine whether the regular simplex is the unique maximizer.

1.2 The adaptive-tilting argument

The analytic input is a Gaussian product inequality for one-dimensional log-concave functions fif_{i} satisfying

∫ℝz​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0,\int_{\mathbb{R}}zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0, (6)

where γk\gamma_{k} denotes standard Gaussian measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}. This condition says that the probability measure proportional to fi​d​γ1f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1} has mean zero. The inequality is a specialization of the centered Gaussian forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb theorem of Milman, Nakamura, and Tsuji [22]; we identify the precise specialization in Section 4 and give a direct proof in Appendix A.

The product inequality cannot be applied directly to the event in (3), because

∫ℝz𝟏(−∞,c](z)dγ1(z)=−ϕ(c).\int_{\mathbb{R}}z\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,c]}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=-\phi(c).

The new step is to choose a separate exponential tilt in each coordinate. Define

r⁡(s)=ϕ⁡(s)Φ⁡(s)=−𝔼⁡[Z∣Z≤s],H⁡(s)=s+r⁡(s)=𝔼⁡[s−Z∣Z≤s].r(s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\Phi(s)}=-\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\leq s],\qquad H(s)=s+r(s)=\mathbb{E}[s-Z\mid Z\leq s]. (7)

The ratio rr is known as the lower-tail inverse Mills ratio [21, 12]. For every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, the function

z⟼er⁡(s)​z𝟏(−∞,s+r(s)](z)z\longmapsto e^{r(s)z}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,s+r(s)]}(z) (8)

has zero Gaussian first moment. The cutoff in (8) is H⁡(s)=s+r⁡(s)H(s)=s+r(s). Choosing different values sis_{i} therefore gives coordinate-dependent cutoffs before the Gaussian change of measure. A strictly concave variational problem chooses s=(si)s=(s_{i}) and a=(r⁡(si))a=(r(s_{i})) so that, for a prescribed c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R},

s+a−R​a=c​𝟏.s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1}. (9)

Here aa is the exponential-tilt parameter and R​aRa is the mean displacement under the correlated Gaussian change of measure. Thus (9) restores the same final threshold cc in every coordinate.

The auxiliary function used in the variational problem is chosen so that ℱ′​(H⁡(s))=r⁡(s)\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(H(s))=r(s): as a function of the shifted endpoint H⁡(s)H(s), it is an antiderivative of the required tilt. The two quadratic penalties are then chosen so that stationarity reproduces both the average tilt and the Gaussian mean displacement R​aRa. This explains the form of the variational functional and leads to the lower bound Φ​(c)m\Phi(c)^{m}.

1.3 Relation to prior work

Rice’s 1950 account of Shannon’s observation and Shannon’s later geometric analysis of Gaussian communication [31, 33] led to work of Balakrishnan [2, 3, 4] and to the low-dimensional argument of Landau and Slepian [17]; Tanner explained the obstruction to extending that argument [38, 39]. Farber’s thesis, Cover’s problem list, and Massey’s Shannon Lecture contain later formulations [10, 9, 20]. The equal-individual-energy Weak Simplex Conjecture is distinct from the average-energy Strong Simplex Conjecture, which Steiner disproved [36].

Later work connected the coding problem to Gaussian maxima and mean width. Litvak summarized the main formulations [18]; Balitskiy, Karasev, and Tsigler developed the Gaussian-noise formulation used here [5]; and Kabluchko, Litvak, and Zaporozhets proved the equivalence between the Gaussian-maximum and mean-width formulations and an asymptotic result [15]. Sun, Hu, and Lan proved the four-variable case [37]. A July 2026 preprint of Guédon and Souli still states the all-dimensional expected-maximum inequality as a conjecture and describes the preceding results as the best known progress [13].

Classical Gaussian comparison and correlation results do not directly give (3). Slepian’s comparison is based on an entrywise covariance order [35]. Pitt’s theorem characterizes association of Gaussian vectors by nonnegative pairwise correlations [27], whereas (2) permits negative off-diagonal entries. The product input used here belongs to the line from the symmetric rectangle and Gaussian correlation inequalities [16, 34, 14, 32, 1] to the forward–reverse framework of Liu, Courtade, Cuff, and Verdú [19], inverse Brascamp–Lieb methods, and centered log-concave extensions [23, 24, 25, 22].

Two earlier preprints announce proofs: Goldsmith for the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture and Pastore for the Weak Simplex Conjecture [11, 26]. Our proof is independent of both. In Appendix B we give a version-specific account of unresolved steps in arXiv:2112.03393v2 and arXiv:2306.13478v2 that prevent us from using their announced conclusions. That discussion concerns only those posted versions and does not rule out repairs or later arguments.

1.4 Scope and organization

The stochastic order is proved for the normalized covariance RR in (4), not for the original covariance GG. For GG we obtain an MGF comparison and, by differentiation at the origin, an expected-maximum comparison. We prove optimal values but do not characterize all optimizers. The finite-energy result concerns deterministic, equiprobable, no-feedback AWGN codes under a maximal per-codeword total-energy constraint, with no bound on the number of channel uses or degrees of freedom.

The proof has four steps. Section 3 derives the maximum-likelihood identity and the covariance normalization. Section 4 isolates the known Gaussian product inequality. Section 5 proves the variational alignment, which is the main new step. Section 6 combines these ingredients by a Gaussian change of measure. The appendices give a direct proof of the product specialization, document the relation to the two prior announced proofs, and supply the rigorous operational reduction for the finite-energy AWGN result.

2 Main results

Throughout, m≥2m\geq 2, 𝟏=(1,…,1)𝖳∈ℝm\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and J=𝟏𝟏𝖳J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}. We write γk\gamma_{k} for standard Gaussian measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}, and ϕ\phi and Φ\Phi for the standard Gaussian density and distribution function. All logarithms are natural. Vector inequalities such as x≤yx\leq y are understood coordinatewise. A correlation matrix is a positive-semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal; it may be singular. For real random variables UU and VV, we write U≤stVU\leq_{\mathrm{st}}V when ℙ{U>t}≤ℙ{V>t}\mathbb{P}\{U>t\}\leq\mathbb{P}\{V>t\} for every t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

Let

𝖬X=max1≤i≤m⁡Xi,𝖬Z=max1≤i≤m⁡Zi,\mathsf{M}_{X}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}X_{i},\qquad\mathsf{M}_{Z}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}Z_{i},

where Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are independent standard Gaussian random variables.

Theorem 2.1.

Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix satisfying

R−1m​J⪰0,R-\frac{1}{m}J\succeq 0,

and let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R). Then

𝖬X≤st𝖬Z.\mathsf{M}_{X}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\mathsf{M}_{Z}. (10)

Equivalently,

ℙ{X≤c𝟏}≥Φ(c)mfor every c∈ℝ.\mathbb{P}\{X\leq c\mathbf{1}\}\geq\Phi(c)^{m}\qquad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}. (11)

The event in (11) is the lower orthant (−∞,c]m(-\infty,c]^{m} with the same threshold in every coordinate. The theorem does not assert the analogous inequality for an arbitrary vector of thresholds.

Corollary 2.2.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, for every nonnegative nondecreasing Borel function ψ\psi,

𝔼​ψ​(𝖬X)≤𝔼​ψ​(𝖬Z),\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{X})\leq\mathbb{E}\psi(\mathsf{M}_{Z}),

and this remains valid when one or both expectations are infinite. In particular, for every λ>0\lambda>0 and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R},

𝔼​eλ​𝖬X≤𝔼​eλ​𝖬Z,𝔼​(𝖬X−t)+≤𝔼​(𝖬Z−t)+.\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\mathsf{M}_{X}}\leq\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\mathsf{M}_{Z}},\qquad\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{M}_{X}-t)_{+}\leq\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{M}_{Z}-t)_{+}.

To state the consequence before normalization, set

G△=mm−1​(I−1m​J).G_{\triangle}=\frac{m}{m-1}\left(I-\frac{1}{m}J\right). (12)

This is the Gram matrix of the vertices of a centered regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex on the unit sphere.

Corollary 2.3.

Let GG be any m×mm\times m correlation matrix, let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G), and let ξ△∼𝒩⁡(0,G△)\xi^{\triangle}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G_{\triangle}). Then

𝔼​exp​{λ​maxi​ξi}≤𝔼​exp​{λ​maxi​ξi△}(λ>0).\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}\right\}\leq\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left\{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}\right\}\qquad(\lambda>0). (13)

No rank assumption is imposed on GG.

Corollary 2.4 (Weak Simplex Conjecture).

Let m=d+1m=d+1, let x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} be unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let the message II be uniform on {1,…,m}\{1,\ldots,m\}. Under the channel

Y=λ​xI+Z,Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),λ>0,Y=\lambda x_{I}+Z,\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),\quad\lambda>0,

the average probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding is no larger than for a regular simplex. Thus a regular simplex is a maximizer for every λ>0\lambda>0.

The comparison in Corollary 2.3 applies to mm unit vectors in any Euclidean space. When the ambient dimension is at least m−1m-1, the regular-simplex value is attainable. In lower dimension it remains a universal upper bound, but the best covariance under the rank constraint is not identified.

Corollary 2.5 (Simplex Mean Width Conjecture).

For every m×mm\times m correlation matrix GG,

𝔼​maxi​ξi≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△=mm−1​𝔼​maxi​Zi.\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}=\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,\mathbb{E}\max_{i}Z_{i}. (14)

Consequently, among all simplices with mm vertices contained in the Euclidean unit ball of ℝm−1\mathbb{R}^{m-1}, a regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex has maximal mean width. More generally, the same conclusion holds in any fixed ambient dimension d≥m−1d\geq m-1 after embedding the regular simplex in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. No uniqueness statement is asserted.

We finally state the finite-energy consequence. Following [28, Definition 1], fix E≥0E\geq 0 and N0>0N_{0}>0 and consider the real AWGN sequence model Y=X+ZY=X+Z, with independent noise coordinates of variance N0/2N_{0}/2. An (E,M,ϵ)(E,M,\epsilon) code has a deterministic encoder with MM equiprobable messages, no feedback, codewords ci∈ℓ2c_{i}\in\ell_{2} satisfying ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E, and an arbitrary decoder with average block error at most ϵ\epsilon. No constraint is imposed on the number of channel uses or nonzero codeword coordinates. For each fixed codebook, equal-prior maximum-likelihood decoding is Bayes-optimal. Let Pc∗​(E,M)P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M) be the largest average correct-decoding probability over such encoders and decoders, and let M∗​(E,ϵ)M^{*}(E,\epsilon) be the largest message size whose error is at most ϵ\epsilon. For M≥2M\geq 2, define

pM​(a)=𝔼​Φ​(W+a)M−1,W∼𝒩⁡(0,1).p_{M}(a)=\mathbb{E}\Phi(W+a)^{M-1},\qquad W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (15)
Corollary 2.6.

In the preceding model, which places no restriction on the number of channel uses, the optimal correct-decoding probability is

Pc∗​(E,M)=pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0),M≥2.P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right),\qquad M\geq 2. (16)

Hence, for 0≤ϵ<10\leq\epsilon<1,

M∗​(E,ϵ)=max⁡({1}∪{M≥2:pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0)≥1−ϵ}).M^{*}(E,\epsilon)=\max\!\left(\{1\}\cup\left\{M\geq 2:p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right)\geq 1-\epsilon\right\}\right). (17)

If 0<ϵ<1−1/M0<\epsilon<1-1/M, there is a unique aM,ϵ>0a_{M,\epsilon}>0 satisfying pM​(aM,ϵ)=1−ϵp_{M}(a_{M,\epsilon})=1-\epsilon, and the minimum energy for MM messages is

Emin​(M,ϵ)=N02​M−1M​aM,ϵ2.E_{\min}(M,\epsilon)=\frac{N_{0}}{2}\frac{M-1}{M}a_{M,\epsilon}^{2}. (18)

For ϵ≥1−1/M\epsilon\geq 1-1/M this minimum is zero, whereas for ϵ=0\epsilon=0 it is infinite.

3 From Gaussian classification to a covariance comparison

We first derive the maximum-likelihood identity and then introduce the normalization that maps the regular-simplex covariance to the identity matrix. Both reductions are standard in the modern literature on the Weak Simplex Conjecture [18, 5].

3.1 The maximum-likelihood integral

Let x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} be unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Conditional on message ii, the density of the observation YY at yy is proportional to

exp⁡(−12​∥y−λ​xi∥2)=exp⁡(−12​∥y∥2−12​λ2+λ⁡⟨y,xi⟩).\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\lVert y-\lambda x_{i}\rVert^{2}\right)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{2}+\lambda\langle y,x_{i}\rangle\right).

Maximum-likelihood decoding therefore selects an index maximizing ⟨y,xi⟩\langle y,x_{i}\rangle. Choose any measurable partition of the tie sets among the maximizing indices. Integrating over the resulting decision regions gives

Pc\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{c}} =1m(2π)−d/2∑i=1m∫Die−∥y−λxi∥2/2dy\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}(2\pi)^{-d/2}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{D_{i}}e^{-\lVert y-\lambda x_{i}\rVert^{2}/2}\,dy
=e−λ2/2m​∫ℝdmaxi⁡eλ​⟨y,xi⟩​d​γd​(y).\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}}{m}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\max_{i}e^{\lambda\langle y,x_{i}\rangle}\,d\gamma_{d}(y). (19)

If Y∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)Y\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and ξi=⟨Y,xi⟩\xi_{i}=\langle Y,x_{i}\rangle, then ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G) for the Gram matrix G=(⟨xi,xj⟩)G=(\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle), and (19) is (1). Linear dependence among the xix_{i} does not affect the identity.

3.2 Adding a common Gaussian random variable

Set

α=m−1m.\alpha=\frac{m-1}{m}. (20)

For a correlation matrix GG, define

R=α​G+1m​J.R=\alpha G+\frac{1}{m}J. (21)

Then RR is a correlation matrix and R−J/m=α​G⪰0R-J/m=\alpha G\succeq 0. Conversely, every correlation matrix satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 2.1 has this form, because

G=α−1​(R−1m​J)G=\alpha^{-1}\left(R-\frac{1}{m}J\right) (22)

is positive semidefinite with unit diagonal.

The transformation has a probabilistic representation. Let ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,G)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,G) and let B∼𝒩⁡(0,1/(m−1))B\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/(m-1)) be independent. Then

Xi=α​(ξi+B),1≤i≤m,X_{i}=\sqrt{\alpha}\,(\xi_{i}+B),\qquad 1\leq i\leq m, (23)

has covariance RR. If μ>0\mu>0 and λ=α​μ\lambda=\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mu, independence of BB gives

e−μ2/2𝔼eμ​𝖬X=e−λ2/2𝔼eλ​maxi​ξi.e^{-\mu^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\mathsf{M}_{X}}=e^{-\lambda^{2}/2}\mathbb{E}e^{\lambda\max_{i}\xi_{i}}. (24)

For G=G△G=G_{\triangle}, (21) gives R=ImR=I_{m}. Thus the regular simplex is represented by independent standard Gaussian coordinates after the normalization.

3.3 The semidefinite condition

The condition R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m is not an entrywise restriction. It is equivalent to

u𝖳​R​u≥1m​(∑i=1mui)2(u∈ℝm),u^{\mathsf{T}}Ru\geq\frac{1}{m}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}u_{i}\right)^{2}\qquad(u\in\mathbb{R}^{m}), (25)

and (22) shows that it is exactly the image of all correlation matrices GG under (21). In particular, negative correlations are allowed. For m=3m=3, take unit vectors x1=e1x_{1}=e_{1}, x2=−e1x_{2}=-e_{1}, and x3=e2x_{3}=e_{2}. The corresponding normalized matrix satisfies

R12=−13,R13=R23=13.R_{12}=-\frac{1}{3},\qquad R_{13}=R_{23}=\frac{1}{3}.

A proof based only on Gaussian association for nonnegative correlations would therefore be insufficient.

The normalization can also change rank. The regular-simplex covariance G△G_{\triangle} has rank m−1m-1, whereas the rank-one term J/mJ/m in (21) maps it to the full-rank matrix ImI_{m}. Conversely, RR may be singular and the associated GG may have any admissible rank. We therefore represent GG by unit vectors in ℝrank⁡G\mathbb{R}^{\rank G} when needed, but state Theorem 2.1 directly in terms of RR.

4 A Gaussian product inequality

Let γ1\gamma_{1} denote standard Gaussian measure on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Appendix A gives an independent proof of Theorem 4.1, and that proof is the input used below. We first identify the result as a specialization of the Gaussian forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb inequality of Milman, Nakamura, and Tsuji [22, Theorem 1.10]. The forward–reverse framework was introduced by Liu, Courtade, Cuff, and Verdú [19]. The centered Gaussian result used here also belongs to the line from Hargé’s convex/log-concave inequality and Royen’s Gaussian correlation theorem [14, 32] to Milman’s inverse Brascamp–Lieb method and the centered results of Nakamura and Tsuji [23, 24, 25]. We use the standard extended-valued convention for log-concavity, so a log-concave function may vanish. A nonzero log-concave function on ℝ\mathbb{R} is automatically Borel measurable.

Theorem 4.1.

Let RR be an m×mm\times m correlation matrix and let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R). For each ii, let fi:ℝ→[0,∞)f_{i}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) be bounded and log-concave, with positive Gaussian integral, and suppose that

∫ℝz​fi​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}}zf_{i}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=0. (26)

Then

𝔼​∏i=1mfi​(Xi)≥∏i=1m∫ℝfi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(X_{i})\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\int_{\mathbb{R}}f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}. (27)

The assertion includes singular RR.

We now spell out the specialization of [22, Theorem 1.10]. In its notation, take I=mI=m, ni=1n_{i}=1, ci=1c_{i}=1, and Σi=1\Sigma_{i}=1 for every input; take a single output with m1=mm_{1}=m, d1=1d_{1}=1, L1=IdℝmL_{1}=\operatorname{Id}_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}, Γ1=R\Gamma_{1}=R, and Q=0Q=0. Set h⁡(x)=∏i=1mfi​(xi)h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(x_{i}). The pointwise hypothesis in that theorem then holds with equality, and its centeredness condition is precisely (26).

It remains only to evaluate the Gaussian constant in that specialization. The constant is

supAi≥0,B⪰0diag⁡(A1,…,Am)⪰Bdet(I+R​B)1/2∏i=1m(1+Ai)1/2.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}A_{i}\geq 0,\ B\succeq 0\\ \diag(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m})\succeq B\end{subarray}}\frac{\det(I+RB)^{1/2}}{\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1+A_{i})^{1/2}}. (28)

Writing A=diag⁡(A1,…,Am)A=\diag(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}) and using B⪯AB\preceq A, Loewner monotonicity of the determinant on positive-definite matrices, Sylvester’s determinant identity, and Hadamard’s inequality give

det(I+R​B)\displaystyle\det(I+RB) =det(I+R1/2​B​R1/2)\displaystyle=\det(I+R^{1/2}BR^{1/2})
≤det(I+R1/2​A​R1/2)\displaystyle\leq\det(I+R^{1/2}AR^{1/2})
=det(I+A1/2​R​A1/2)\displaystyle=\det(I+A^{1/2}RA^{1/2})
≤∏i=1m(1+Ai),\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1+A_{i}),

because Ri​i=1R_{ii}=1. Thus the constant in (28) is at most one; taking A=B=0A=B=0 shows that it is exactly one. The general theorem permits the output covariance Γ1=R\Gamma_{1}=R to be singular. Hence it yields (27), including the singular case, with no loss in the constant.

Condition (26) says that the probability measure proportional to fi​d​γ1f_{i}\,d\gamma_{1} has mean zero. The independent proof in Appendix A uses the classical symmetric rectangle inequality, normalized self-convolution, and the central limit theorem. The general proof in [22] also uses normalized self-convolutions and the central limit theorem. Including the direct proof keeps the precise input, including singular covariances, self-contained.

The theorem cannot be applied directly to (11). The indicator f(z)=𝟏(−∞,c](z)f(z)=\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,c]}(z) is log-concave, but

∫z​f​(z)​d​γ1​(z)=−ϕ⁡(c)≠0.\int zf(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z)=-\phi(c)\neq 0.

An exponential tilt can impose condition (26) in one coordinate. Under a correlated Gaussian change of measure, however, the threshold in coordinate ii moves by (R​a)i(Ra)_{i}. We must therefore choose all tilts together so that their first moments vanish and their shifted thresholds all equal the prescribed value cc.

5 Adaptive tilting

Fix c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. We construct a positive tilt vector aa and a threshold vector ss satisfying

s+a−R​a=c​𝟏,s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1},

together with the variational estimate needed in the proof of Theorem 2.1.

5.1 The one-dimensional calculation

Lemma 5.1.

Let a>0a>0 and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R}, put fa,b(z)=ea​z𝟏(−∞,b](z)f_{a,b}(z)=e^{az}\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,b]}(z), and set s=b−as=b-a. Then

∫fa,b​d​γ1\displaystyle\int f_{a,b}\,d\gamma_{1} =ea2/2​Φ​(s),\displaystyle=e^{a^{2}/2}\Phi(s), (29)
∫z​fa,b​(z)​d​γ1​(z)\displaystyle\int zf_{a,b}(z)\,d\gamma_{1}(z) =ea2/2​(a​Φ​(s)−ϕ⁡(s)).\displaystyle=e^{a^{2}/2}\bigl(a\Phi(s)-\phi(s)\bigr). (30)

In particular, the second integral vanishes if and only if

a=r⁡(s),b=s+r⁡(s)=H⁡(s).a=r(s),\qquad b=s+r(s)=H(s). (31)
Proof.

Completing the square gives

ea​z​ϕ​(z)=ea2/2​ϕ​(z−a).e^{az}\phi(z)=e^{a^{2}/2}\phi(z-a).

Integration over (−∞,b](-\infty,b] proves (29). Differentiating that integral with respect to aa, while holding bb fixed, proves (30). Its vanishing is equivalent to a=ϕ⁡(s)/Φ⁡(s)=r⁡(s)a=\phi(s)/\Phi(s)=r(s), and then b=s+a=H⁡(s)b=s+a=H(s). ∎

For s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, let rr and HH be defined by (7). Direct differentiation gives

r′​(s)=−r⁡(s)​H​(s)<0.r^{\prime}(s)=-r(s)H(s)<0. (32)

𝔼⁡[Z∣Z≤s]=−r⁡(s),𝔼⁡[Z2∣Z≤s]=1−s​r​(s).\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\leq s]=-r(s),\qquad\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}\mid Z\leq s]=1-sr(s).

t1+t2​ϕ​(t)≤Φ⁡(−t)≤ϕ⁡(t)t,t>0.\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\phi(t)\leq\Phi(-t)\leq\frac{\phi(t)}{t},\qquad t>0.

5.3 The variational construction

Assume that RR satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, and define GG by (22). Choose unit vectors x1,…,xm∈ℝdx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where d=rank⁡Gd=\rank G, such that

We therefore evaluate ℱ\mathcal{F} at affine functions of (q,v)(q,v). The quadratic terms below are chosen so that stationarity in vv gives v=∑iai​xiv=\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}, which produces the correlated displacement R​aRa, while stationarity in qq gives the average-tilt relation q=c+a¯q=c+\bar{a}.

on

𝒟={(q,v):q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩>0​ for all ​i}.\mathcal{D}=\left\{(q,v):q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle>0\text{ for all }i\right\}. (40)

The set 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a nonempty open convex set; for example, (q,0)∈𝒟(q,0)\in\mathcal{D} for every q>0q>0.

Proposition 5.2.

The functional 𝒥c\mathcal{J}_{c} has a unique maximizer (q∗,v∗)∈𝒟(q_{*},v_{*})\in\mathcal{D}. Because HH is a bijection, there are unique si∈ℝs_{i}\in\mathbb{R} satisfying

H⁡(si)=q∗+α⁡⟨xi,v∗⟩.H(s_{i})=q_{*}+\alpha\langle x_{i},v_{*}\rangle. (41)

With ai=r⁡(si)a_{i}=r(s_{i}), these variables satisfy

s+a−R​a=c​𝟏s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1} (42)

and

∑i=1mlog⁡Φ⁡(si)+12​a𝖳​(I−R)​a≥m​log⁡Φ⁡(c).\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\Phi(s_{i})+\frac{1}{2}a^{\mathsf{T}}(I-R)a\geq m\log\Phi(c). (43)
Proof.

Strict concavity follows from (36) and the strictly concave quadratic part of (39). We give the attainment argument explicitly. Set

L=𝒥c​(H⁡(c),0)−1andK={(q,v)∈𝒟:𝒥c​(q,v)≥L}.L=\mathcal{J}_{c}(H(c),0)-1\quad\text{and}\quad K=\{(q,v)\in\mathcal{D}:\mathcal{J}_{c}(q,v)\geq L\}.

α2​∥v∥2+m2​(q−c)2≤−L,\frac{\alpha}{2}\lVert v\rVert^{2}+\frac{m}{2}(q-c)^{2}\leq-L,

so KK is bounded. Suppose that a sequence in KK converges to a boundary point of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. At least one quantity q+α​⟨xi,v⟩q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle then tends to zero. By (37), the corresponding term in (39) tends to −∞-\infty; all other ℱ\mathcal{F} terms are nonpositive and the quadratic terms stay bounded. This contradicts the definition of KK. Hence the closure of KK in ℝ×ℝd\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} is contained in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. It follows that KK is compact. Since points outside KK have value below LL, whereas 𝒥c​(H⁡(c),0)>L\mathcal{J}_{c}(H(c),0)>L, the global maximum is attained in KK, hence in the interior of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Strict concavity makes it unique.

Define sis_{i} by (41) and set ai=r⁡(si)=ℱ′​(H⁡(si))>0a_{i}=r(s_{i})=\mathcal{F}^{\prime}(H(s_{i}))>0. With yi=q+α⁡⟨xi,v⟩y_{i}=q+\alpha\langle x_{i},v\rangle, the two derivatives are

a𝖳​R​a\displaystyle a^{\mathsf{T}}Ra =α​∥∑iai​xi∥2+1m​(∑iai)2\displaystyle=\alpha\lVert\textstyle\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}\rVert^{2}+\frac{1}{m}\left(\sum_{i}a_{i}\right)^{2}

The variables have distinct roles: sis_{i} determines the interval endpoint, ai=r⁡(si)a_{i}=r(s_{i}) is the exponential tilt, and R​aRa is the displacement of the correlated Gaussian vector. Allowing the sis_{i} to differ is what makes the common final threshold in (42) possible.

We first record the Gaussian change-of-measure identity in a form that also covers singular covariance matrices.

Lemma 6.1.

Let X∼𝒩⁡(0,R)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R) for a positive-semidefinite matrix RR. For every a∈ℝma\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and every nonnegative Borel function F:ℝm→[0,∞]F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to[0,\infty],

=∫ℝkF⁡(T⁡(u+t))​d​γk​(u)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}F(T(u+t))\,d\gamma_{k}(u)
=𝔼​F​(X+T​T𝖳​a).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}F(X+TT^{\mathsf{T}}a).

This is (46). No inverse of RR is required. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

Fix c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} and let s,as,a be supplied by Proposition 5.2. Put

bi=si+aib_{i}=s_{i}+a_{i} (47)

and define

7 Coding and geometric consequences

7.1 Moment-generating functions

Proof of Corollary 2.3.

Let RR be defined from GG by (21). By Corollary 2.2,

𝔼​eμ​𝖬X≤𝔼​eμ​𝖬Z(μ>0).\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\mathsf{M}_{X}}\leq\mathbb{E}e^{\mu\mathsf{M}_{Z}}\qquad(\mu>0).

Use (24) on the left. On the right, R=ImR=I_{m} is the image of G△G_{\triangle} under (21), so the same identity applied in reverse gives (13), with λ=α​μ\lambda=\sqrt{\alpha}\,\mu. As μ\mu ranges over (0,∞)(0,\infty), so does λ\lambda. ∎

The stochastic order in Theorem 2.1 concerns the normalized covariance RR. It does not imply maxiξi≤stmaxiξi△\max_{i}\xi_{i}\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle} for the original covariance GG. What transfers through (24) is the MGF comparison (13).

7.2 Equal-energy Gaussian classification

Proof of Corollary 2.4.

For the Gram matrix GG of the code, (19) writes the success probability as the MGF appearing in Corollary 2.3, multiplied by a factor independent of the code. The covariance G△G_{\triangle} is realized by a regular simplex in ℝm−1=ℝd\mathbb{R}^{m-1}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. Applying (13) proves the result for every λ>0\lambda>0. ∎

7.3 Expected maxima and mean width

Proof of Corollary 2.5.

A finite maximum of Gaussian random variables has exponential moments of its absolute value. In particular, for some δ>0\delta>0, 𝔼⁡[|maxi⁡ξi|​eδ​|maxi⁡ξi|]<∞\mathbb{E}[|\max_{i}\xi_{i}|e^{\delta|\max_{i}\xi_{i}|}]<\infty, and the analogous bound holds for ξ△\xi^{\triangle}. Dominated convergence therefore differentiates both MGFs at λ=0\lambda=0. They equal one there, so taking right derivatives in (13) gives

𝔼​maxi​ξi≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△.\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle}.

If Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are independent and Z¯=m−1​∑iZi\bar{Z}=m^{-1}\sum_{i}Z_{i}, then

ξi△=dmm−1​(Zi−Z¯).\xi_{i}^{\triangle}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}(Z_{i}-\bar{Z}).

Taking maxima and expectations proves the equality in (14).

We next pass from vertices on the sphere to arbitrary simplices in the unit ball. Let y1,…,ym∈B2dy_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\in B_{2}^{d}, let e1,…,eme_{1},\ldots,e_{m} be orthonormal and orthogonal to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and define

xi=(yi,1−∥yi∥2​ei).x_{i}=\left(y_{i},\sqrt{1-\lVert y_{i}\rVert^{2}}\,e_{i}\right).

The vectors xix_{i} are unit vectors in ℝd+m\mathbb{R}^{d+m}. This increase of ambient dimension is harmless because Corollary 2.3 imposes no rank restriction. If g∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)g\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and W1,…,WmW_{1},\ldots,W_{m} are independent standard Gaussian random variables, then conditional Jensen’s inequality gives

𝔼​maxi​⟨g,yi⟩\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\langle g,y_{i}\rangle ≤𝔼​maxi⁡(⟨g,yi⟩+1−∥yi∥2​Wi)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\left(\langle g,y_{i}\rangle+\sqrt{1-\lVert y_{i}\rVert^{2}}\,W_{i}\right)
≤𝔼​maxi​ξi△,\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\max_{i}\xi_{i}^{\triangle},

where the second inequality is (14) applied to the unit vectors xix_{i}.

Let K=conv⁡{y1,…,ym}K=\conv\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\}, let hKh_{K} be its support function, and let σd−1\sigma_{d-1} be normalized rotation-invariant measure on the unit sphere. We use the convention

w⁡(K)=∫Sd−1(hK​(u)+hK​(−u))​d​σd−1​(u)=2​∫Sd−1hK​(u)​d​σd−1​(u).w(K)=\int_{S^{d-1}}\bigl(h_{K}(u)+h_{K}(-u)\bigr)\,d\sigma_{d-1}(u)=2\int_{S^{d-1}}h_{K}(u)\,d\sigma_{d-1}(u).

Writing a standard Gaussian vector as the product of its norm and its independent uniform direction gives

𝔼​hK​(g)=𝔼​∥g∥2​w​(K).\mathbb{E}h_{K}(g)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\lVert g\rVert}{2}\,w(K). (53)

Thus, in a fixed ambient dimension, the expected-maximum comparison is exactly a comparison of mean widths. Taking d=m−1d=m-1 proves the stated mean-width inequality for simplices. When d≥m−1d\geq m-1, the regular simplex may be embedded in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and the same argument applies there. ∎

7.4 The finite-energy AWGN formula

Proof of Corollary 2.6.

The detailed operational reduction is given in Appendix C. We summarize the argument. The likelihood ratios of the MM Gaussian shift measures are measurable with respect to at most M−1M-1 Gaussian linear statistics, obtained from an orthonormal basis of the codeword-difference span. These statistics are sufficient even though the infinite white-noise output is not an ℓ2\ell_{2}-valued random vector.

A code with ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E may then be embedded isometrically with one additional signal coordinate so that every codeword has energy exactly EE; the decoder may ignore that coordinate, so optimal performance cannot decrease. In the finite sufficient-statistic experiment, the equal-energy means have a common radius r≤Er\leq\sqrt{E} in a space of dimension at most M−1M-1. The maximum-likelihood identity and Corollary 2.3 bound their correct-decoding probability by that of a regular (M−1)(M-1)-simplex of radius rr. The smaller-radius simplex experiment is an explicit message-independent Gaussian degradation of the larger-radius experiment, so its optimal correct-decoding probability is no larger [6]. Hence the radius-E\sqrt{E} regular simplex is optimal.

Represent the feasible centered simplex as {ui−u¯:1≤i≤M}\{u_{i}-\bar{u}:1\leq i\leq M\}, where the uiu_{i} are pairwise orthogonal and have norm E​M/(M−1)\sqrt{EM/(M-1)}. The vectors uiu_{i} themselves may have energy larger than EE; they are used only as an equivalent translated representation for evaluating the decoding probability. Translating every signal and the observation by the common vector u¯\bar{u} leaves the statistical experiment unchanged. Conditioning on the noise in the transmitted coordinate then yields

Pc∗​(E,M)=𝔼​Φ​(W+E​M/(M−1)N0/2)M−1,W∼𝒩⁡(0,1),P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=\mathbb{E}\Phi\!\left(W+\frac{\sqrt{EM/(M-1)}}{\sqrt{N_{0}/2}}\right)^{M-1},\qquad W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),

which is (16). Equation (17) follows from the definition of M∗M^{*}. Finally, pMp_{M} is continuous and strictly increasing, with pM​(0)=1/Mp_{M}(0)=1/M and pM​(a)↑1p_{M}(a)\uparrow 1 as a→∞a\to\infty. Solving (16) for EE proves (18) and its endpoint cases. ∎

This is the deterministic, equiprobable, no-feedback model with an arbitrary decoder, a maximal per-codeword total-energy constraint, and no restriction on the number of channel uses, as in [28, Definition 1]. It establishes the fixed-(M,ϵ)(M,\epsilon) simplex-code assertion discussed in [29, Remark 21.2].

8 Discussion and open problems

The proof combines a known Gaussian product inequality subject to a vanishing Gaussian first-moment condition with a new adaptive tilting step. The product inequality alone does not compare the interval indicators needed for an equal-threshold lower orthant. The variational problem couples the coordinate conditions ai=r⁡(si)a_{i}=r(s_{i}) to the covariance through s+a−R​a=c​𝟏s+a-Ra=c\mathbf{1}, which makes every coordinatewise threshold equal to cc after the Gaussian change of measure.

Open problem 8.1.

Determine the equality cases in (11), (13), and the coding and mean-width consequences. In particular, determine when equality at one nontrivial threshold or one positive MGF parameter forces R=ImR=I_{m}, or equivalently forces the original covariance to be G△G_{\triangle} after (21).

The present argument does not answer this question. Strict concavity of the variational functional gives a unique aligning tilt for fixed RR and cc, but it neither supplies the equality cases of the product inequality nor shows that every optimal code is regular.

A second open direction is the rank-constrained problem. For mm unit vectors in dimension d<m−1d<m-1, Corollary 2.3 gives the regular (m−1)(m-1)-simplex value as a universal upper bound, but the regular simplex is not feasible in the prescribed dimension. Identifying the best covariance of rank at most dd is a separate problem.

Another question is whether the adaptive tilting method extends to unequal thresholds, unequal marginal variances, or other one-sided log-concave factors. None of these extensions follows from the auxiliary function used here. In particular, the argument does not prove the stronger Gaussian-measure conjectures of Balitskiy–Karasev–Tsigler [5], Guédon–Souli Conjecture 1.7 [13], or conjectures concerning Gaussian minima and other intrinsic volumes.

For communication, (17) is restricted to the model stated in Corollary 2.6. Feedback, stop-feedback, average-over-codebook energy, randomized encoding under weaker constraints, unequal priors, and non-Gaussian noise require different arguments. The false Strong Simplex Conjecture shows that the change from individual to average energy is substantive [36].

The main conclusion can be stated without coding terminology: every correlation matrix satisfying R⪰J/mR\succeq J/m produces a Gaussian maximum that is stochastically dominated by the maximum of independent standard Gaussian variables. The adaptive tilts supply the threshold compatibility that turns the product inequality into this comparison.

Appendix A A direct proof of the Gaussian product inequality

This appendix proves Theorem 4.1 from the symmetric Gaussian rectangle inequality. The argument uses normalized self-convolution and the central limit theorem. More general centered Gaussian correlation and forward–reverse Brascamp–Lieb inequalities are proved in [24, 25, 22].

A.1 Symmetric rectangles and even functions

We begin with the classical Šidák–Khatri inequality in the form needed below [16, 34]. For a recent refinement and a related strong Gaussian correlation conjecture, see [1].

Lemma A.1.

Let V=(V1,…,Vm)V=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{m}) be a centered Gaussian vector with Var⁡(Vi)=1\operatorname{Var}(V_{i})=1 for every ii. For r1,…,rm∈[0,∞]r_{1},\ldots,r_{m}\in[0,\infty],

ℙ{|Vi|≤ri for all i}≥∏i=1mℙ{|Z|≤ri},Z∼𝒩(0,1).\mathbb{P}\{|V_{i}|\leq r_{i}\text{ for all }i\}\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq r_{i}\},\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (54)
Proof.

By monotone convergence, it is enough to prove the assertion when every rir_{i} is finite; the cases ri=∞r_{i}=\infty follow by increasing finite radii to infinity. Suppose first that the covariance is positive definite, and proceed by induction on mm. For m=1m=1, the two sides are equal. For the induction step, let

A=∏i<m[−ri,ri].A=\prod_{i<m}[-r_{i},r_{i}].

Conditionally on Vm=tV_{m}=t, the first m−1m-1 coordinates have the form Y+b​tY+bt, where YY is a centered Gaussian vector independent of VmV_{m} and bb is fixed. Set

q(t)=ℙ{Y+bt∈A}.q(t)=\mathbb{P}\{Y+bt\in A\}.

Symmetry of AA and YY makes qq even. Prékopa’s theorem [30, 8] shows that qq is log-concave, because it is the marginal of the jointly log-concave function

(t,y)⟼𝟏A​(y+b​t)​ϕY​(y).(t,y)\longmapsto\mathbf{1}_{A}(y+bt)\phi_{Y}(y).

An even log-concave function on ℝ\mathbb{R} is nonincreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Therefore q⁡(Vm)q(V_{m}) and 𝟏{|Vm|≤rm}\mathbf{1}_{\{|V_{m}|\leq r_{m}\}} are both nonincreasing functions of |Vm||V_{m}|. For independent copies W,W′W,W^{\prime} and two functions u,vu,v that are monotone in the same direction,

2​Cov⁡(u⁡(W),v⁡(W))=𝔼⁡[(u⁡(W)−u⁡(W′))​(v⁡(W)−v⁡(W′))]≥0.2\operatorname{Cov}(u(W),v(W))=\mathbb{E}[(u(W)-u(W^{\prime}))(v(W)-v(W^{\prime}))]\geq 0.

Applying this identity with W=|Vm|W=|V_{m}| gives

ℙ{V∈A×[−rm,rm]}\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\{V\in A\times[-r_{m},r_{m}]\} =𝔼q(Vm)𝟏{|Vm|≤rm}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}q(V_{m})\mathbf{1}_{\{|V_{m}|\leq r_{m}\}}
≥𝔼q(Vm)ℙ{|Z|≤rm}.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}q(V_{m})\,\mathbb{P}\{|Z|\leq r_{m}\}.

The first factor is the (m−1)(m-1)-coordinate rectangle probability, so the induction hypothesis completes the positive-definite case.

Now let the covariance matrix RR be singular. Let W∼𝒩⁡(0,Im)W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}) be independent of VV and define

V(ε)=1−ε​V+ε​W,Rε=(1−ε)​R+ε​Im.V^{(\varepsilon)}=\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}\,V+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,W,\qquad R_{\varepsilon}=(1-\varepsilon)R+\varepsilon I_{m}.

Then RεR_{\varepsilon} is positive definite and V(ε)→VV^{(\varepsilon)}\to V almost surely. The boundary of the rectangle in (54) is contained in the finite union of sets {|Vi|=ri}\{|V_{i}|=r_{i}\} over indices with ri<∞r_{i}<\infty. Every marginal is standard Gaussian, so this boundary has probability zero. Bounded convergence proves the singular case. ∎

Lemma A.2.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma A.1, let g1,…,gm:ℝ→[0,∞)g_{1},\ldots,g_{m}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty) be bounded, even, and log-concave. Then

𝔼​∏i=1mgi​(Vi)≥∏i=1m∫gi​d​γ1.\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}(V_{i})\geq\prod_{i=1}^{m}\int g_{i}\,d\gamma_{1}. (55)
Proof.

Each strict superlevel set of an even log-concave function on ℝ\mathbb{R} is an interval centered at the origin, possibly empty or unbounded. Empty sets contribute zero, and an unbounded interval is obtained from bounded symmetric intervals by monotone convergence. The layer-cake formula, Tonelli’s theorem, and Lemma A.1 give

𝔼​∏i=1mgi​(Vi)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\prod_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}(V_{i}) =∫[0,∞)mℙ{gi(Vi)>ti for all i}dt1⋯dtm\displaystyle=\int_{[0,\infty)^{m}}\mathbb{P}\{g_{i}(V_{i})>t_{i}\text{ for all }i\}\,dt_{1}\cdots dt_{m}
≥∫[0,∞)m∏i=1mℙ{gi(Z)>ti}dt1⋯dtm\displaystyle\geq\int_{[0,\infty)^{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{P}\{g_{i}(Z)>t_{i}\}\,dt_{1}\cdots dt_{m}
=∏i=1m𝔼​gi​(Z).\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}g_{i}(Z).

∎

Appendix B Relation to two prior announced proofs

Goldsmith [11] and Pastore [26] announce proofs of the Simplex Mean Width and Weak Simplex conjectures, respectively. We record why we do not use the current posted versions as prior proofs. The discussion concerns only arXiv:2112.03393v2, revised 27 June 2023, and arXiv:2306.13478v2, revised 13 November 2023. All page, section, theorem, and equation references below refer to those versions. It is not a claim that either conjecture is false, that either strategy cannot be repaired, or that the authors have no later argument.

B.1 Goldsmith’s centroid-monotonicity step

The dependency in [11] is

Theorem 3.1⟹Corollary 3.2⟹Theorem 4.1.\text{Theorem 3.1}\Longrightarrow\text{Corollary 3.2}\Longrightarrow\text{Theorem 4.1}.

Theorem 3.1 is a strict monotonicity statement for spherical centroids under a longitudinal shift. On pp. 7–9, its proof uses local approximations and reduces the pointwise Prékopa–Leindler hypothesis to a sufficient inequality. At the end of p. 9, the manuscript observes that this inequality fails as the dimension tends to infinity and derives only a restricted angular condition. The proof then ends without another estimate verifying the required pointwise hypothesis. Corollary 3.2 invokes Theorem 3.1, and Theorem 4.1 invokes Corollary 3.2. Thus the posted argument does not establish the claimed all-dimensional theorem.

B.2 Pastore’s centroid-injectivity step

The injectivity argument in Section III-D of [26] defines conditional means tt and t′t^{\prime} over the differences D~∖D~′\widetilde{D}\setminus\widetilde{D}^{\prime} and D~′∖D~\widetilde{D}^{\prime}\setminus\widetilde{D} in (18c)–(18d). The appendix obtains the set inclusions (23b)–(23c) and then treats the means as points of the corresponding differences when deriving the sign statements (24b)–(24c). A conditional mean belongs to the closed convex hull of its support, not necessarily to the support itself, and a difference of convex cones need not be convex. The failed inequality in (24b) or (24c) may depend on the sampled point and need not survive averaging.

The issue occurs within the Gaussian simplicial-cone setting. In ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} let

where a>0a>0. Then

ℙ{Gc∈D}=∏j=13Φ(cj/σ).\mathbb{P}\{G_{c}\in D\}=\prod_{j=1}^{3}\Phi(c_{j}/\sigma).

As a function of qj=cj2q_{j}=c_{j}^{2}, the logarithm of each factor is strictly concave: its derivative is proportional to r⁡(qj/σ)/qjr(\sqrt{q_{j}}/\sigma)/\sqrt{q_{j}}, which is strictly decreasing. Symmetry and strict concavity therefore give the unique centroid cD=(1,1,1)/3c_{D}=(1,1,1)/\sqrt{3}. If Xσ=cD+σ​ZX_{\sigma}=c_{D}+\sigma Z, conic homogeneity and dominated convergence imply

1σ​𝔼​[Xσ∣Xσ∈A1/4]⟶𝔼⁡[Z∣Z∈A1/4]∈int⁡D1/4′.\frac{1}{\sigma}\mathbb{E}[X_{\sigma}\mid X_{\sigma}\in A_{1/4}]\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Z\in A_{1/4}]\in\operatorname{int}D^{\prime}_{1/4}.

Thus, for all sufficiently large σ\sigma, the conditional mean in (18c), with the relevant Gaussian centroid, lies in D1/4′D^{\prime}_{1/4} rather than in D∖D1/4′D\setminus D^{\prime}_{1/4}. The sign conclusions (24b)–(24c), used in (19)–(20) to prove injectivity, therefore do not follow.

There is a second, independent issue in the same appendix. It asserts that the oriented facet normals e1,ei,ei′e_{1},e_{i},e_{i}^{\prime} are pairwise linearly independent, so every coefficient in λ1​e1+λi​ei+λi′​ei′=0\lambda_{1}e_{1}+\lambda_{i}e_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{\prime}e_{i}^{\prime}=0 is nonzero and one may normalize λ1=1\lambda_{1}=1 before defining the partition in (22). Let

V~=(u1,u2,u3),V~′=(u1+u32,u2,u3),\widetilde{V}=(u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}),\qquad\widetilde{V}^{\prime}=\left(\frac{u_{1}+u_{3}}{\sqrt{2}},u_{2},u_{3}\right),

where u1,u2,u3u_{1},u_{2},u_{3} are the standard basis. Both triples are linearly independent and differ only in their first generator. For i=2i=2,

span⁡(u1,u3)=span⁡(u1+u32,u3),\operatorname{span}(u_{1},u_{3})=\operatorname{span}\!\left(\frac{u_{1}+u_{3}}{\sqrt{2}},u_{3}\right),

so the corresponding oriented normals satisfy e2=e2′=u2e_{2}=e_{2}^{\prime}=u_{2}. The valid dependence e2−e2′=0e_{2}-e_{2}^{\prime}=0 has λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, and the normalization and case partition in (22) do not cover this admissible configuration.

Both issues occur in the injectivity result used in Section III-E to deduce reflection symmetry. They are independent of the present proof. We therefore cite [11, 26] as prior announced proofs but do not use their asserted conclusions.

Appendix C Operational reduction for finite-energy AWGN

We justify the reduction used in Corollary 2.6. The channel is the real AWGN sequence model

Y=X+Z,Zj∼iid𝒩⁡(0,N0/2).Y=X+Z,\qquad Z_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,N_{0}/2). (71)

The encoder is deterministic, the MM messages are equiprobable, there is no feedback, and every codeword ci∈ℓ2c_{i}\in\ell_{2} satisfies ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E. The decoder is arbitrary, and there is no constraint on the number of channel uses or nonzero codeword coordinates. This is the finite-energy model of [28, Definition 1].

The output sequence ZZ is almost surely not an element of ℓ2\ell_{2}, so one cannot literally project the whole observation onto a Hilbert subspace. The finite family of Gaussian shift measures nevertheless has a finite-dimensional sufficient statistic, which is the reduction needed below.

C.1 Finite-dimensional sufficient statistics

Work on the canonical output space

Ω=ℝℕ,𝒜=ℬ​(ℝ)⊗ℕ,\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}},\qquad\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})^{\otimes\mathbb{N}},

with coordinate maps Yk​(y)=ykY_{k}(y)=y_{k}. Let PiP_{i} be the product Gaussian law on (Ω,𝒜)(\Omega,\mathcal{A}) when cic_{i} is transmitted, and set

D=span⁡{ci−c1:1≤i≤M}⊂ℓ2.D=\operatorname{span}\{c_{i}-c_{1}:1\leq i\leq M\}\subset\ell_{2}.

Choose an orthonormal basis u1,…,uru_{1},\ldots,u_{r} of DD, where r≤M−1r\leq M-1, and define the measurable partial sums

Sj,n​(y)=∑k=1nuj,k​yk.S_{j,n}(y)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{j,k}y_{k}.

We use one measurable version of the limit for all hypotheses:

Tj​(y)={limn→∞Sj,n​(y),if the limit exists,0,otherwise,1≤j≤r.T_{j}(y)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}S_{j,n}(y),&\text{if the limit exists},\\[4.30554pt] 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad 1\leq j\leq r. (72)

The convergence set is Borel and the limit there is a pointwise limit of measurable functions, so TjT_{j} is 𝒜\mathcal{A}-measurable.

Under message ii, write Yk=ci,k+ZkY_{k}=c_{i,k}+Z_{k}. The deterministic series ∑kuj,k​ci,k\sum_{k}u_{j,k}c_{i,k} converges by Cauchy–Schwarz. The random series ∑kuj,k​Zk\sum_{k}u_{j,k}Z_{k} consists of independent centered Gaussian variables and

∑k=1∞Var⁡(uj,k​Zk)=N02​∑k=1∞uj,k2=N02.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Var}(u_{j,k}Z_{k})=\frac{N_{0}}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}u_{j,k}^{2}=\frac{N_{0}}{2}.

It therefore converges almost surely and in L2​(Pi)L^{2}(P_{i}). Thus (72) is a common version under every PiP_{i}, and

T⁡(Y)∼𝒩⁡((⟨ci,uj⟩)j=1r,N02​Ir)under ​Pi.T(Y)\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left((\langle c_{i},u_{j}\rangle)_{j=1}^{r},\frac{N_{0}}{2}I_{r}\right)\qquad\text{under }P_{i}. (73)

For di=ci−c1d_{i}=c_{i}-c_{1}, write di=∑j=1rβi​j​ujd_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\beta_{ij}u_{j} and define

⟨Y,di⟩:=∑j=1rβi​j​Tj​(Y).\langle Y,d_{i}\rangle:=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\beta_{ij}T_{j}(Y).

Under every hypothesis this agrees almost surely with limn∑k=1ndi,k​Yk\lim_{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}d_{i,k}Y_{k}. The Cameron–Martin formula [7] gives

Li​(Y):=d​Pid​P1​(Y)=ℓi​(T⁡(Y)),L_{i}(Y):=\frac{dP_{i}}{dP_{1}}(Y)=\ell_{i}(T(Y)), (74)

where

ℓi​(t)=exp⁡{2N0​∑j=1rβi​j​tj−1N0​(∥ci∥2−∥c1∥2)}.\ell_{i}(t)=\exp\!\left\{\frac{2}{N_{0}}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\beta_{ij}t_{j}-\frac{1}{N_{0}}\bigl(\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}-\lVert c_{1}\rVert^{2}\bigr)\right\}. (75)

For completeness, if Li,nL_{i,n} is the likelihood ratio based on the first nn coordinates, then (Li,n)n(L_{i,n})_{n} is a nonnegative P1P_{1}-martingale and

supn𝔼P1​Li,n2≤exp⁡(2​∥di∥2N0)<∞.\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}_{P_{1}}L_{i,n}^{2}\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{2\lVert d_{i}\rVert^{2}}{N_{0}}\right)<\infty.

Hence Li,nL_{i,n} converges in L1​(P1)L^{1}(P_{1}) to the expression in (74). In particular, every likelihood ratio is measurable with respect to T=(T1,…,Tr)T=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{r}).

Let ℓ1≡1\ell_{1}\equiv 1 and let P¯=M−1​∑i=1MPi\overline{P}=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{M}P_{i} be the output law under the uniform prior. Bayes’ formula gives

ℙ⁡{I=i∣Y}=ℓi​(T​(Y))∑k=1Mℓk​(T⁡(Y))P¯​-almost surely.\mathbb{P}\{I=i\mid Y\}=\frac{\ell_{i}(T(Y))}{\sum_{k=1}^{M}\ell_{k}(T(Y))}\qquad\overline{P}\text{-almost surely}. (76)

Thus a Bayes-optimal decoder, equivalently a maximum-likelihood decoder under the uniform prior, is a deterministic function of TT. Conversely, every decoder based on TT is also a decoder based on the full output. The sequence experiment and the finite-dimensional Gaussian experiment (73) therefore have the same optimal probability of correct decoding.

C.2 Reduction to a regular simplex at full energy

Proposition C.1.

Among all MM-message codes in the preceding model, the optimal average probability of correct decoding is attained by a centered regular (M−1)(M-1)-simplex whose vertices have squared norm EE.

Proof.

Start with arbitrary codewords c1,…,cM∈ℓ2c_{1},\ldots,c_{M}\in\ell_{2} satisfying ∥ci∥2≤E\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}\leq E. Append one independent signal/noise coordinate; after relabeling the countable coordinates, this is the isometric embedding ℓ2↪ℓ2⊕ℝ≅ℓ2\ell_{2}\hookrightarrow\ell_{2}\oplus\mathbb{R}\cong\ell_{2}. Set

c~i=(ci,E−∥ci∥2).\widetilde{c}_{i}=\left(c_{i},\sqrt{E-\lVert c_{i}\rVert^{2}}\right). (77)

Every augmented codeword has squared norm EE. A decoder in the augmented experiment may ignore the additional observation coordinate and use the original decoder. Thus optimal correct-decoding probability cannot decrease under this augmentation.

Let

D~=span⁡{c~i−c~1:1≤i≤M}.\widetilde{D}=\operatorname{span}\{\widetilde{c}_{i}-\widetilde{c}_{1}:1\leq i\leq M\}.

By the sufficient-statistic construction above, the augmented experiment is equivalent to a Gaussian shift experiment on D~\widetilde{D}. All c~i\widetilde{c}_{i} have the same orthogonal projection ww onto D~⟂\widetilde{D}^{\perp}. Write

c~i=w+vi,vi∈D~.\widetilde{c}_{i}=w+v_{i},\qquad v_{i}\in\widetilde{D}. (78)

The sufficient statistics have means viv_{i}; the common component ww does not appear. Since w⟂D~w\perp\widetilde{D} and the c~i\widetilde{c}_{i} have equal norm,

∥vi∥2=E−∥w∥2=:r2\lVert v_{i}\rVert^{2}=E-\lVert w\rVert^{2}=:r^{2} (79)

is independent of ii, with 0≤r≤E0\leq r\leq\sqrt{E}, and dimD~≤M−1\dim\widetilde{D}\leq M-1.

If r>0r>0, apply Corollary 2.3 and the maximum-likelihood identity to the unit vectors vi/rv_{i}/r, after identifying D~\widetilde{D} with a Euclidean space and embedding it in ℝM−1\mathbb{R}^{M-1} if necessary. Their probability of correct decoding is no larger than that of a regular (M−1)(M-1)-simplex of radius rr. If r=0r=0, all finite-dimensional means coincide and the optimal probability is 1/M1/M.

It remains to compare radii. Let 0≤r1≤r20\leq r_{1}\leq r_{2}, put σ2=N0/2\sigma^{2}=N_{0}/2, and consider a fixed regular simplex x1,…,xMx_{1},\ldots,x_{M}. If r2>0r_{2}>0, set η=r1/r2\eta=r_{1}/r_{2}. From the observation Y2=r2​xI+σ​ZY_{2}=r_{2}x_{I}+\sigma Z, form

K⁡(Y2)=η​Y2+σ​1−η2​Z′,K(Y_{2})=\eta Y_{2}+\sigma\sqrt{1-\eta^{2}}\,Z^{\prime}, (80)

where Z′Z^{\prime} is an independent standard Gaussian vector. Conditional on II, K⁡(Y2)K(Y_{2}) has the same law as r1​xI+σ​Z′′r_{1}x_{I}+\sigma Z^{\prime\prime}. Thus the radius-r1r_{1} experiment is a message-independent randomized degradation of the radius-r2r_{2} experiment. Composing a decoder for the former with this kernel may produce a randomized decoder for the latter. Randomization cannot improve Bayes success for finitely many hypotheses under zero–one loss: conditional on an observation, success is a linear function of the decision probabilities and is maximized by a deterministic maximum-a-posteriori rule. The optimal deterministic probability is therefore nondecreasing in rr. This is also an instance of the Blackwell comparison principle [6]. A regular simplex of radius E\sqrt{E} is feasible and attains the resulting upper bound. ∎

The equalization step uses the maximal energy constraint on each codeword. It does not yield the same conclusion under an average-over-codebook energy constraint.

C.3 Evaluation of the simplex decoding probability

Let e1,…,eMe_{1},\ldots,e_{M} be the standard basis of ℝM\mathbb{R}^{M} and set

A=E​MM−1,ui=A​ei,u¯=1M​∑j=1Muj.A=\sqrt{\frac{EM}{M-1}},\qquad u_{i}=Ae_{i},\qquad\bar{u}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}u_{j}. (81)

The centered vectors ui−u¯u_{i}-\bar{u} form a feasible regular simplex and

∥ui−u¯∥2=A2​(1−1M)=E.\lVert u_{i}-\bar{u}\rVert^{2}=A^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right)=E. (82)

The orthogonal representatives uiu_{i} have squared norm E​M/(M−1)>EEM/(M-1)>E when M>1M>1 and are not asserted to be feasible codewords. They are used only to evaluate the equivalent translated experiment: adding the common vector u¯\bar{u} to every signal and to the observation is a deterministic bijection and leaves all likelihood ratios and optimal decoding probabilities unchanged.

Suppose message 11 is sent and write σ=N0/2\sigma=\sqrt{N_{0}/2}. In the orthogonal representation, correct maximum-likelihood decoding occurs when

A+σ​W1≥σ​Wj(2≤j≤M),A+\sigma W_{1}\geq\sigma W_{j}\qquad(2\leq j\leq M),

for independent standard Gaussian random variables W1,…,WMW_{1},\ldots,W_{M}. Conditioning on W1=WW_{1}=W gives

Pc∗​(E,M)=𝔼​Φ​(W+Aσ)M−1=pM​(2​E​M(M−1)​N0).P_{\mathrm{c}}^{*}(E,M)=\mathbb{E}\Phi\!\left(W+\frac{A}{\sigma}\right)^{M-1}=p_{M}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2EM}{(M-1)N_{0}}}\right). (83)

By symmetry this is also the average success probability, proving (16).

For completeness, pMp_{M} from (15) is continuous and

pM′​(a)=(M−1)​𝔼​[Φ​(W+a)M−2​ϕ​(W+a)]>0.p_{M}^{\prime}(a)=(M-1)\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Phi(W+a)^{M-2}\phi(W+a)\right]>0. (84)

At a=0a=0, the random variable Φ⁡(W)\Phi(W) is uniform on (0,1)(0,1), so pM​(0)=1/Mp_{M}(0)=1/M. Dominated convergence gives pM​(a)↑1p_{M}(a)\uparrow 1 as a→∞a\to\infty. These facts prove the assertions about aM,ϵa_{M,\epsilon} and EminE_{\min} in Corollary 2.6. They also show that the set in (17) has a largest element. For fixed EE, the shift 2​E​M/((M−1)​N0)\sqrt{2EM/((M-1)N_{0})} remains bounded as M→∞M\to\infty, whereas the maximum of M−1M-1 independent standard Gaussian random variables diverges in probability. Therefore the correct-decoding probability tends to zero.
